terms.SOLID principles: SOLID bundles five principles popularized by Robert C. Martin: single responsibility (one actor or reason to change per module), open/closed (extend behavior without editing stable code), Liskov substitution (subtypes honor base contracts), interface segregation (clients depend only on what they use) and dependency inversion (policy and detail both depend on abstractions owned by the policy side). They overlap: dependency inversion enables open/closed, and interface segregation is single responsibility for interfaces. They trade simplicity for flexibility, so apply them where change actually happens. In Python, protocols, first-class functions and modules often satisfy them with less ceremony than class hierarchies.
terms.Liskov substitution principle: Formalized by Liskov and Wing as behavioral subtyping: a subtype must not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, break invariants, or allow state changes the base type forbids (the history rule). Type checkers verify signatures only, so behavioral violations pass static analysis. Typical breaks: overriding a method to raise NotImplementedError, returning None instead of a promised list, or narrowing accepted inputs. Fixes include immutable designs, inverting the hierarchy (read-only base, mutable subtype, as in collections.abc Sequence and MutableSequence) or replacing inheritance with composition and a shared protocol. LSP is what makes polymorphism, and therefore open/closed, safe.
terms.Dependency injection: DI supplies collaborators from outside, usually via constructor parameters (preferred), method parameters or setters. Wiring happens once at the composition root, such as main() or an app factory. It enables deterministic tests by injecting fakes for clocks, randomness, networks and storage, without monkeypatching. DI is a technique; dependency inversion is the design principle it typically serves, and injecting concrete classes still couples you to details. Python rarely needs containers: default arguments and factories suffice, while FastAPI's Depends and pytest fixtures provide framework-level injection. Avoid the service locator, which looks dependencies up from a global registry and hides them again.
terms.Design pattern: The term comes from Christopher Alexander's architecture work and was brought to software by the Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides) in 1994: 23 patterns, 5 creational, 7 structural, 11 behavioral. Each pattern has a name, problem, solution and consequences. Patterns are communication tools; the same code shape can be different patterns depending on intent, as with Adapter, Decorator and Proxy. In dynamic languages many patterns shrink to idioms: functions replace Strategy and Command classes, and generators replace Iterator. Overuse is a known failure mode; introduce a pattern when a real axis of change appears.
terms.Singleton pattern: A singleton combines two concerns: a single instance (lifetime) and global access (visibility). The second causes the damage: hidden dependencies, order-dependent initialization and tests that contaminate each other. Hand-written lazy initialization can race under threads. Python alternatives: a module-level instance (modules are created once per interpreter), a cached factory with functools.cache that tests can reset with cache_clear(), or creating the object at the composition root and injecting it. DI containers express the same lifetime as a 'singleton scope' while keeping access explicit. Legitimate uses include process-wide pools and hardware handles.
terms.Factory method pattern: In the GoF form, a base class defines an overridable creation method used by its own logic, so subclasses choose the concrete product while the surrounding algorithm stays unchanged. In common usage, 'factory' also covers simple factory functions, alternative constructors (classmethods like datetime.fromisoformat) and registries keyed by name, often populated with decorators or __init_subclass__ for plugins. Distinguish it from Abstract Factory, which groups several creation methods so a family of products stays consistent. Pitfalls: factories for types that never vary, string keys that fail only at runtime, and products lacking a common interface.
terms.Builder pattern: Builder separates step-by-step construction from the final representation, validating invariants once in build(). Fluent builders return self so calls chain. The GoF version includes a director that drives the steps, allowing one process to produce different representations. It suits immutable objects, many optional parameters and cross-field constraints. In Python, keyword-only arguments, dataclasses with __post_init__ checks and pydantic models usually replace explicit builders; query builders (SQLAlchemy's select().where()) and test data builders remain common. Watch for mutable builders reused across calls, and builders whose build() skips validation and lets half-configured objects escape.
terms.Decorator pattern: A GoF decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped component, forwards calls and adds responsibilities before or after. Wrappers compose, replacing a combinatorial explosion of subclasses with n small classes, but order changes semantics: caching outside retries differs from retries outside caching. Python's @ syntax is sugar for f = deco(f) and applies the concept to functions; functools.wraps preserves metadata. lru_cache and cached_property are built-in examples. A decorator must be transparent to callers, keeping return types and exceptions consistent, or it violates Liskov substitution. Deep stacks complicate stack traces and add call overhead.
terms.Strategy pattern: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a shared interface and lets the client select one, typically by composition. It is the standard cure for type-based if/elif chains and an implementation of open/closed. In Python a strategy is usually any callable: functions, lambdas, functools.partial, or objects with __call__; classes help when strategies carry configuration or several methods. Strategy and State share structure but differ in who switches: the client picks a strategy, while states switch themselves. Strategy versus Template Method is composition versus inheritance for varying one step. Strategies make table-driven tests of business rules straightforward.
terms.Observer pattern: Observer sets up one-to-many notification: the subject holds subscribers and calls them on change, in push style (data sent along) or pull style (observers query back). Publish-subscribe adds a broker so parties are fully decoupled and delivery can be asynchronous or cross-process. Pitfalls: lapsed listeners that leak memory (use weak references or explicit unsubscribe), one failing observer stopping the rest, reentrancy when callbacks mutate the subject, unspecified ordering, and cascades that obscure control flow. Iterate over a copy of the subscriber list. Reactive libraries such as ReactiveX generalize Observer into composable event streams.
terms.Code smell: Coined by Kent Beck and popularized in Fowler's Refactoring, a smell is a heuristic symptom, not a defect. The catalog includes long function, large class, duplicated code, long parameter list, feature envy, data clumps, primitive obsession, shotgun surgery, divergent change, speculative generality, message chains and magic numbers. Each maps to refactoring moves, such as Extract Function, Move Function, Introduce Parameter Object or Replace Conditional with Polymorphism. Tools detect some smells: linters (ruff, pylint) and complexity metrics (radon's cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity). Judge in context: a long but linear function can be clearer than ten fragments.
terms.Refactoring: Fowler defines refactoring as a behavior-preserving change to internal structure, done in small, named, verifiable steps. The workflow: start green, make one move, run tests, commit; on red, revert rather than debug. Keep refactoring commits separate from feature commits so reviewers can verify no behavior changed. For untested legacy code, Feathers recommends finding seams and adding characterization tests first. Large migrations use the strangler fig pattern, branch by abstraction or parallel change (expand, migrate, contract). IDE automated refactorings (rename, extract, inline) are safer than manual edits, and mutation testing can check whether the test net is strong enough.
